sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry today, with near normal temperatures.
- Precipitation chances increasing across higher terrain Friday afternoon. Becoming widespread Saturday afternoon into Sunday.
- A drying and warming trend will set in Monday, through at least midweek.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: This afternoon will feature warmer temps and increasing high- clouds in southwesterly flow aloft. Temperatures this afternoon will be around 60 degrees in lower elevations of SW-Idaho and in the 50s in the Oregon high desert and higher Idaho basins. A weak shortwave will move northeast over the area this evening. While moisture availability remains somewhat limited, sufficient moisture will advect northward to south-central Idaho to support isolated to scattered showers late Thursday night through Friday. As this shortwave departs, a brief dry period will occur Friday night, barring a continued 20-50% chance of precipitation in the far eastern portions of our CWA.

Come Halloween, a closed low with an elongated southern trough will begin encroaching upon our area. Ahead of this trough, a good pull of Pacific moisture will overspread our area, allowing for precipitable water values to reach around the 90th percentile in southwest Idaho. This moisture will allow for increasing precipitation chances across the area through Saturday, peaking Saturday evening and night (60-90% chance, highest in SW-Idaho) as the greatest forcing for ascent overspreads our area. The day shift made a good argument for a Mary Poppins costume, as an umbrella would make a good addition to any costume for evening festivities. Over the course of Saturday evening through Sunday, liquid precipitation totals are generally 0.5-1 inch in northern mountains, 0.20-0.50 inches in lower elevations and southern mountains, and then 0.01 to 0.20 in eastern Oregon.

The southwesterly flow aloft will keep snow-levels elevated to 6.5- 8.5 kft MSL with the bulk of the precipitation, limiting snow accumulations across the area. While they will eventually lower to 3.5-5kft MSL behind the cold front, which passes through the area Sunday, this will coincide with as precipitation tapers off behind the departing system. This will keep much of the snow above 6.5kft MSL, with totals trending down with the snow levels trending higher. Over the course of the same period above, elevations above 6.5kft MSL would see a dusting to a few inches of snow (although the highest peaks in the Sawtooths could see several).

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Showers will continue through Sunday, tapering off throughout the day as the system departs, with QPF details in the short-term. Snow levels Sunday will have lowered to 4.5-6.5kft MSL (increasing from west to east), allowing for a chance of snow/wintry mix down to around 4.5 kft MSL Sunday in E-Oregon, with little to no accumulation expected that low. Sunday afternoon and evening will feature gusty winds following the cold frontal passage, with west to northwest gusts of 20-40 mph (strongest in the typical windy portions of the Snake River Plain.

Beginning Monday, the area will be dry with a warming trend through Thursday, although seasonable temperatures are anticipated throughout. While there will be multiple opportunities for weak shortwaves to pass over the area, moisture will be limited and the shortwaves will just result in periods of increased high clouds.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and mostly dry through the work week.
- Unsettled weather returns late this weekend and early next week. Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during this time. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: SW flow aloft will be over the area Thu thru Fri. A weak disturbance will be embedded in the flow on Fri. However, it appears most of the moisture with this feature will stay mainly to the east, with only a slight chc of showers over he far nern plains. Temperatures both days will stay in the 60's over the plains.

By Sat, little change is expected as SW flow aloft remains over the area. There appears to be a weak disturbance embedded in the flow which may bring a chc of showers to portions of the higher terrain. Temperatures will remain in the 60's over nern CO.

Looking ahead to Sun and Sun night, there continues to be a lot of uncertainty as to how an upper level trough over the Pacific NW evolves. The ECMWF has this feature moving southeast with a closed low developing over the Great Basin by Sun night. Meanwhile, the GFS has the system moving more east southeast with a closed low over swrn WY by Sun night. Ahead of this feature, both models do have an influx of subtropical moisture with an increasing chc of showers over the higher terrain late Sun aftn thru Sun night. Over the plains, a sfc lee trough will extend from ern WY into ern CO with southerly low level flow. Most of the plains will be dry thru Sun aftn, but shower activity may gradually increase Sun night.

For early next week, the ECMWF has an upper level low near the 4 corners area by 12z Mon which moves east southeast across nrn New Mexico thru late Mon aftn. Meanwhile, the GFS has the upper level low over swrn WY moving east southeast across central CO into sern CO by late Mon aftn. As a result, these two differing solutions lead to varying amounts of precipitation over the area. The ECMWF solution would keep the heavier precipitation focused over srn CO while the GFS solution would focus further north over nern CO.

Furthermore, the fcst continues complicated for Mon night into Tue as the ECMWF has the upper level low moving southeast into wrn Texas while the GFS has the upper level low over central Kansas. The ECMWF solution would have precipitation ending over most of the area by 12z Tue while the GFS solution would have lingering precipitation thru Tue aftn over portions of the plains. In addition, both models do have a shot of cooler air moving in Mon thru Mon night which could change some of the rain to snow late Mon night into Tues morning at lower elevations. However, ensemble data from both models only show very light accumulations below 6000 ft if the rain does change to snow. To complicate things even further, the Canadian solution keeps the track of the main upper level low well to the north of the area from late Sun night thru Tue morning. As a result, it has very little precipitation across the area due to its northern track. Thus, there remains a tremendous amount of uncertainty as to how things will develop Sun night thru Tue.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep through the area Sunday night, bringing colder and windier conditions into the area for Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry, warm, and breezy conditions are expected to continue through Thursday, with mild overnight lows.
- Chances for a few showers return Saturday (Halloween) with temperatures remaining mild.
- A pattern change to colder, wetter, and windier conditions is favored Sunday into Tuesday, but the details remain highly uncertain at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A fairly quiet end to the work week is expected across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. Upper-level flow will remain southwesterly throughout the day Thursday and Friday as an upper- level trough strengthens off the West Coast and a ridge builds across the central CONUS. Weak 700mb flow develops with the building ridge, with temperatures increasing into the 3 to 5C range throughout the afternoon Thursday. Surface temperatures are expected to warm to the upper-50s to mid-60s across the region with no precipitation expected at this time. Overnight lows Thursday into Friday will drop into the mid-30s to mid-40s, a fairly mild night for this time of year. Surface winds will remain mostly light, around 10 to 15 mph, throughout the day Thursday. This will result in a quite pleasant fall day for much of the area, so be sure to get outside and enjoy it!

Friday will be another mild day as southwesterly flow remains in place as the upper-level trough off the coast of the Pacific Northwest slowly moves inland. A weak, upper-level shortwave is currently progged to move northeastward out of the Four Corners region towards the CWA throughout the day Friday. This shortwave looks to push through the region between 21Z Friday and 03Z Saturday. This system will be quite weak by the time it reaches the CWA, with minimal associated 500mb vorticity with the shortwave. The 700mb shortwave will be very diffuse by the time it reaches southeast Wyoming later Friday evening, however, it should still provide some weak ascent across portions of the CWA. Weak 700mb warm air advection with further support some forcing, though it too will be quite weak. 700mb temperatures will top out around 6C for portions of the area. With the passing shortwave, there will be a slight chance for PoPs across the region. Significant precipitation is not anticipated and all precipitation looks to fall as rain and not snow, given the warmer 700mb temperatures. High temperatures on Friday will be in the mid-50s to mid-60s, with the Nebraska Panhandle likely being the cooler location due to overcast skies for much of the day. Overnight lows will decrease into the mid-30s to mid-40s, with the Panhandle remaining warmer due to the increased cloud coverage across the area.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes. Please see previous discussion...

Most of the area will see pleasant conditions for Halloween trick-or- treating this year. Broad ridging will remain over the area this weekend, supporting above average high temperatures ranging from the upper 50s in Carbon and Albany counties to the low to mid 60s over the High Plains. Expect a mix of cloud cover and sunshine as plentiful moisture moves over the area aloft. A weak vort-max passing through the area in the southwest flow overhead will help to support a few afternoon and evening showers, mainly over and near the higher terrain, but the chance for appreciable rainfall or thunder is low. Due to high humidity and cloud cover, overnight low temperatures will be mild for this time of year, only dropping to the upper 30s to lower 40s east of I-25, and mid to upper 30s to the west. Near saturated conditions will produce the potential for some spooky fog to develop both Saturday morning and Saturday night. Sunday looks mild again, but slightly cooler than Saturday with skies becoming mostly cloudy ahead of the next storm system approaching the area.

A complex storm system will push across the western CONUS Sunday into early next week. Two major players will make up this system: first, a strong, moisture-laden upper level low riding the subtropical jet stream into the southwest and second, a potent Pacific trough pushing into the northwest. The primary questions concerning the evolution of this system are if, when, and where the two approaching systems might merge together. Ensembles have shifted slightly over the last 24 hours, but have yet to converge on a solution. Thus, several scenarios still remain, though the probabilities have changed. In the first scenario (approx 40% chance), the two features do not merge at all. Two separate mid- level circulations competing with one other would mean muddy forcing forcing for ascent and limited precipitation potential. We could still expect some rain and snow showers, but amounts would be modest (0.25" or less for Laramie, Cheyenne, Wheatland, Scottsbluff, 0.25" to 0.5" in Rawlins and Chadron). In the second scenario (approx 50% chance), the two systems merge, but this occurs a little too late and a little too far east for a widespread major precipitation event for our area. Still, it would be enough for a moderate rain event over western Nebraska, and some potential for accumulating snow especially for the elevated ridges (Cheyenne Ridge & Pine Ridge). The scenario in which the two systems merge early enough to produce a major event has decreased in probability (to around 10%) as fewer ensembles now show this potential. The ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index for QPF today has decreased slightly as well to around 0.5 to 0.6 over much of the area. This tells us that while an anomalous event is still possible, only a small subset of ensemble members show this, keeping confidence low.

Overall probabilities for 0.5" of liquid precipitation are the lowest around Laramie, Cheyenne, and Wheatland (30-40%). Probabilities increase both east and west, with Rawlins around a 50% chance to exceed 0.5" and the Sidney to Chadron corridor in the 60 to 70% range. In addition to the uncertainty in QPF, there is also uncertainty in the snow levels with very marginal temperatures for snow over much of the area. Cooler air moving in through the event should lead to snow levels starting fairly high (perhaps 9000 ft) and then dropping overnight Sunday night and through the day Monday. The question is how low they can get. Thus, there is fairly good confidence in accumulating snow for the mountains (90+% chance for 1" and 50% chance for 6"), but lower confidence around where most folks live. The best chances for 1" or more of snow outside of the mountains are in the valleys of Carbon and Albany counties, and the elevated ridges of the High Plains.

Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep through the area Sunday night, bringing colder and windier conditions into the area for Monday. Which of the above scenarios that ends up playing out will also affect the wind direction and potential for high winds. Still, there is high confidence in a windy day along and east of the Laramie range. About 25% of ensemble members have 700-mb winds sufficiently high to support widespread high wind potential, while the I-80 summit area has about a 50% chance for high winds. Look for lingering impacts in the form of cool temperatures and windy conditions on Tuesday, but we should start to lose the wind and warm up slightly by Wednesday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Additionally, a cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 ft by Monday morning, and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation chances return Friday with light rain at the lower elevations and flurries above 10,000 ft.
- Deeper moisture arrives Saturday night and will increase the chances for impactful precipitation for southwest CO Sunday and Monday.
- Flooding/Flash Flooding remains a concern, especially along vulnerable terrain or areas that have saturated soils from last week's rain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A low pressure system continues to drop down the West Coast today. This will transition the parent flow to southwesterly, which will advect upper level moisture into the region. This will increase cloud cover over the coming days, but keeps the moisture confined to those upper levels. Therefore, a pleasant fall day is on tap today.
ISOLATED TO SCATTERED SHOWERS FRIDAY AND SATURDAY:

A wave rotating around the parent low will provide enough lift to kick off showers beginning Friday afternoon and lasting through Saturday. PWAT values are projected to be upwards of 200% of normal, although dry surface levels will take time to fully saturate. Precipitation totals through Saturday will be on the lighter side as a result, with predominantly rain showers, with some snow flurries possible above 10,000 ft. There is a possibility for a few stray thunderstorms, which would be capable of producing localized heavier rainfall across the region.
WETTER AND UNSETTLED BY SUNDAY AND MONDAY:

A stronger moisture push associated with an atmospheric river (AR) arrives by Sunday. This AR will begin taking a southern track through Baja California, propagating through the Desert Southwest. There continues to be disagreements between both the ECMWF and GFS models. The ECMWF insists on bringing the moisture plume further north, while the GFS confines the highest PWATs to the Four Corners region. Therefore, there are still some uncertainties when it comes to the extent of this moisture. Either way, this is an impressive amount of moisture that, when combined with enhanced lift ahead of an approaching low, will result in widespread precipitation. Models do still agree on an area of 1-2 inches of rainfall across southwest Colorado and southeast Utah Sunday into Monday. Chances for river flooding remains low at this point, as these totals will be spread over an almost 48 hour period. The bigger concern lies with flash flooding across areas with already saturated soils from last week's rainfall, particularly for areas of steep terrain, and over recent burn scars. See the Hydrology section below for additional information.

Additionally, a cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 ft by Monday morning, and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front. Snow could be heavy at times. Mountain passes will likely see impacts, with some travel slowdowns for motorists Monday morning and into the afternoon. Precipitation will taper off Monday night, with colder and drier conditions anticipated Tuesday and beyond. Daytime highs on Monday and Tuesday will run close to 10 degrees below normal, with temperatures remaining in this range through much of next week.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Regardless, latest models show plenty of moisture moving into the mountains through Sunday, with activity spreading east onto the plains through Tuesday. Temperatures will also cool off another 10- 15 degrees or so by then thanks to an influx of cooler air.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and warm today, with some morning fog over the plains.
- Potential for mountain snow and heavy rain returns to the Continental Divide this weekend, spreading over the San Luis Valley as well into Monday.
- Mountain snow increases early next week, with showers spreading east across the area. Parts of the forecast are still uncertain.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Be on the lookout for patchy fog over the eastern plains during the early morning, mainly east of Pueblo County, with coverage increasing closer to the KS border. Visibility will drop off quickly in these areas, so exercise caution when traveling. Fog should clear up later this morning, by about 10am or so.

One last mild and quiet day today before our next system starts moving in. Thanks to the recent cold front, temperatures will be a few degrees cooler today, with 50s to mid-60s across most of the area, though a few places over the southern plains may hit 70 this afternoon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Much more active weather is expected to move into the region starting on Friday, and lasting into early next week.

On Friday, a deep upper low will slowly move down along the west coast, while a secondary low moves towards California, getting embedded in a broad upper trough. Flow aloft over our region will pick up out of the southwest, bringing good moisture transport into the mountains. Showers will be isolated to scattered in nature to begin with, mainly falling over the San Juans. Meanwhile, a shortwave will pass over the southern portion of our CWA, which could bring some scattered afternoon showers to the far eastern plains. That will most likely depend on the speed of the wave as it pushes past, with most of the heavier accumulations falling in Kansas and the OK Panhandle.

Moving into the weekend, the forecast gets less certain as model solution begin to diverge. The general trends have the northern low pushing southeast towards Nevada into Sunday, while the southern low moves onshore in California. Beyond this point, the two low pressures will phase with the broad flow pattern, namely the deepening trough over the western CONUS, before pushing east and into our area. That being said, the exact timing, path, and amplitude of the systems as they interact are still too wildly different between solutions for any fine details to be decided on just yet.

In spite of the wide arrange of synoptic patterns we could see into early next week, the trend of impacts has started to take shape. QPF spread amongst latest guidance shows the highest accumulations in the San Juans, no surprise there given the persistent SW flow, followed by the central mountains, with the rest of the higher terrain varying a bit more. Snow levels are still uncertain, given that even a subtle shift north or south of the approaching low could impact how much cold air moves into the region. In general, we can expect heavier snow over the San Juans, mainly closer to the peaks. Uncertainty increases even more looking further east, as the path of the system will greatly influence whether the Palmer Divide and eastern plains receive any precipitation at all, with deterministic guidance varying considerably.

Regardless, latest models show plenty of moisture moving into the mountains through Sunday, with activity spreading east onto the plains through Tuesday. Temperatures will also cool off another 10- 15 degrees or so by then thanks to an influx of cooler air. Beyond that, models still need more time to agree on the details.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Drier conditions quickly build in on Monday as the weather system exits to our east, with much cooler conditions expected in its wake. High pressure is expected to prevail across the region through at least the middle half of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Tropical moisture moving into the region on Friday will lead to scattered showers and thunderstorms capable of producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding, mainly across southwest Utah.
- A strong atmospheric river will interact with a potent northern stream trough Sunday into Monday, resulting in widespread moderate to heavy precipitation across the region.
- Cooler air moves in behind a strong cold front that will bring snow levels as low as 6500 feet with accumulating mountain snow.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Our region is currently under the influence of dry southwesterly flow courtesy of a longwave troughing pattern off the west coast. This trough is expected to deepen along the coast on Friday as a northern stream cutoff low digs southward, introducing more moist, southerly flow aloft that will tap into what is currently Tropical Storm Vance. Concurrently, a shortwave is expected to eject northeastward through the region around the eastern periphery of the parent trough, introducing modest amounts of instability that will aid in the development of widely scattered showers and thunderstorms throughout the day. Storms are expected to develop mid to late morning first across southwest Utah, with coverage expanding northward through the day as moisture fills into the region. Particularly across southwest Utah, where deepest moisture and instability is maximized, flash flooding will be a risk. Current high-res guidance shows a bullseye of heaviest precipitation concentrated around Zion NP and the southern mountains, with a 75% chance of accumulations exceeding 0.3-0.8" Friday into Saturday morning, and a 25% chance for accumulations to exceed 0.8-1.3" in these areas. Elsewhere, accumulations are expected to be on the lighter side, between a few hundredths of an inch upwards of 0.25".

There will be a relative lull in storm activity on Sunday as subsidence behind the exiting shortwave fills in. Given some lingering moisture, there is some potential for some more isolated shower activity in the afternoon and evening, but overall conditions remain dry for holiday festivities.

On Sunday, the aforementioned northern stream cutoff low will phase with a Pacific low and shift inland. Confidence is increasing for this system to bring widespread moderate to heavy precipitation between Sunday and Monday morning. Two distinct areas of heaviest precipitation are evident in recent guidance: one across southwest Utah, attributed to the associated atmospheric river that will bring deep moisture and instability across southern Utah, and one across northern Utah, attributed to a period of heavy precipitation accompanying a cold front passage on Sunday. QPF amounts have increased overall, with even low-end guidance indicating likely chances (75%+) for widespread precipitation accumulations between 0.5-1" between Sunday and Monday morning. Accumulations across southwest Utah, the Wasatch Front, and all Utah mountains will likely see accumulations closer to 1.5-2" with localized areas seeing upwards of 3".

The cold front associated with the northern stream trough will usher in a much cooler airmass late Sunday into Monday morning. Snow levels will gradually decrease from 9500 feet late Sunday to around 6500-7000 feet early Monday. As such, accumulating mountain snow is expected through this period, with generally 3-6 inches expected with upwards of 12-18 inches along the higher elevations.

Drier conditions quickly build in on Monday as the weather system exits to our east, with much cooler conditions expected in its wake. High pressure is expected to prevail across the region through at least the middle half of next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
